vignette:
He is 76 now, a South Asian man who has spent most of his life working as an electrician, the kind of person who still notices loose wires, overloaded sockets, and the faint buzz behind a wall. He has been married for decades, and he speaks about his life as one built on routine, work, and responsibility. Even after slowing down in recent years, he continues to take small jobs through old contacts, preferring to keep his hands busy rather than sit idle. Before the robbery, he describes himself as careful but not fearful. He took pride in being independent, in carrying cash when needed, in traveling across familiar neighborhoods without giving it much thought.

The robbery happens in the early evening, after a day spent repairing lighting in a small shop. He is walking back toward his car with his tools and payment tucked into his jacket. He notices two younger men near the corner but does not think much of it at first. Then one of them steps in front of him and the other comes from behind. He remembers the sudden closeness of their bodies, the smell of sweat, the sharp command to hand everything over. One of them shoves him hard enough that he loses balance. His tool bag drops. He sees a flash of metal in one man’s hand—not even clearly, just enough for his mind to decide it is a knife. In that instant he is certain he may die there on the pavement over a day’s wages and an old phone.

He gives them his wallet and the cash. Even after that, one of them strikes him across the side of the head. What stays with him is not only the pain but the humiliation of it, the sense that he has been reduced from a respected elder and skilled tradesman to someone helpless. He remembers lying still for a few seconds after they run, hearing traffic continue as if nothing unusual has happened. Later, when he gets home, his wife cries harder than he does. He tells her he is lucky, that nothing worse happened, but his hands shake as he says it.

In the first weeks afterward, he cannot stop replaying the scene. At night, just as he begins to drift off, he sees again the movement of the man stepping into his path. He wakes with his heart pounding, sometimes reaching toward the bedside lamp before he is fully conscious. He becomes alert to sounds he used to ignore—footsteps outside, a scooter slowing near the house, voices behind him in a shop. He starts checking the gate repeatedly before bed. If his wife asks whether he locked it already, he becomes irritated, insisting he is only being sensible.

He tells himself he should be over it. Instead, his world gets smaller. He turns down evening electrical jobs and makes excuses to old customers. He no longer wants to carry tools after dark. If he must go out, he scans every face, especially young men standing in pairs. In crowded markets, he positions himself with his back to a wall and keeps one hand pressed to his pocket even when there is nothing valuable in it. He avoids the street where the robbery happened, taking longer routes that add unnecessary time and frustration to his day. His wife notices that he startles when she approaches him from behind in the kitchen. Once, when his grandson runs up and grabs his arm unexpectedly, he jerks away so sharply that the child begins to cry.

He feels ashamed of these reactions. In his mind, a man who has raised a family, migrated, worked with live current, and solved practical problems all his life should not be undone by a few minutes on a sidewalk. That thought makes him quieter. He shares less with his children because he does not want them to think he has become weak with age. Yet his wife sees the change. He sits more often by the window, watching who passes. He keeps retelling certain details of the robbery but goes blank when she asks how frightened he was. When sleep is poor, he becomes short-tempered the next day, snapping over minor things and then withdrawing into silence.

What troubles him most in the present is how persistent the sense of danger feels. He knows, rationally, that the men are gone and the robbery is over. Still, his body does not seem to believe it. When he reaches into a fuse box in a dim stairwell or enters a vacant corridor for a repair, he feels a rush of tension that has little to do with electricity. He listens for footsteps before he can focus on the job. He has begun to wonder whether the world has changed, or whether he has. Around others, he tries to appear normal—competent, composed, still himself. But privately, he feels as though something was stolen that evening beyond his wallet: his ease in ordinary life, his confidence in familiar streets, and his trust that attention and experience are enough to keep him safe.
